analysis.one_liner: Protects workers from being fired or punished for reporting federal law violations and waste.
analysis.headline: Rep. Barbara Boxer's bill to shield employees who report federal law violations died in committee with zero cosponsors and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for any employer to fire, demote, or otherwise punish a worker for reporting violations of federal law, refusing to break the law, or helping an employer comply with it. It covered reports of fraud, mismanagement, waste of federal funds, abuse of authority, and dangers to public health or safety tied to federal programs and contracts. Workers could file a complaint with the Secretary of Labor, get an investigation within 90 days, and win back pay, reinstatement, and possibly punitive damages. It was referred to committee, sent to two subcommittees, and never came up for a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees — including private-sector workers, federal contractors' employees, and state and local government workers — who witness violations of federal law, waste, abuse of authority, or threats to public health and safety connected to federal programs. The bill would have given them a Labor Department complaint process, a 90-day investigation, protection from retaliation, and a path to reinstatement, back pay with interest, attorney's fees, and possibly punitive damages.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Whistleblowers at federal contractors and agencies

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any employer from taking or threatening unfavorable personnel actions against an employee who makes a protected disclosure, helps achieve compliance with federal law, or refuses to violate federal law.

Gives workers a complaint route to the Secretary of Labor, who must investigate within 90 days and can order interim relief enforceable immediately if there is reasonable cause to believe the complaint has merit.
Provides real remedies: reinstatement with seniority, back pay with interest, compensation for special damages including litigation costs and attorney's fees, and possible punitive damages.

Shifts the burden of proof to the employer: once a worker shows protected activity was a contributing factor in the punishment, the employer must prove by clear and convincing evidence it would have acted the same way anyway.

Covers a wide range of workers, including state and local government employees, and protects disclosures of mismanagement, gross waste of funds, abuse of authority, and substantial and specific dangers to public health or safety.

analysis.who_pays: Employers whose operations touch federal programs, contracts, or authority — including federal contractors and grant recipients, and state and local governments as employers. They would face Labor Department investigations, hearings, reinstatement and back-pay orders, attorney's fees, and possible punitive damages when they retaliate against whistleblowers, plus the cost of defending complaints built on a worker's reasonable belief of mismanagement or waste.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal contractors and employers who retaliate

drawbacks.text: The bill's remedies would supersede, and replace, existing federal rights and remedies for the same conduct, which could leave some workers with a narrower set of protections than current law gives them.

Protected disclosures include a worker's 'reasonable belief' of mismanagement or gross waste of funds — broad categories that could generate costly, disputed complaints for employers even when no actual violation exists.
The bill applies to state and local governments as employers, which would expose them to federal complaints and damages for personnel decisions, raising federalism and administrative-cost objections.

The Department of Labor would take on new investigation and hearing duties with fixed deadlines (90 days to investigate, 180 days for an administrative law judge decision), with cases spilling into the courts when those deadlines are missed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a worker facing an illegal order or seeing waste of public money, the bill offered strong, practical protection: a fast investigation, immediate interim relief, and real money damages with the burden of proof on the employer. The main design concerns are the supersession of other federal remedies, which could trade away some existing protections, and the breadth of 'reasonable belief' disclosures, which shifts litigation risk onto employers. Weighed against the value of making it safe to report fraud and safety dangers in federally funded work, the protections are substantial and the costs are the ordinary price of enforceable rights.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the Education and Labor Committee, then forwarded to two subcommittees, and died there when the Congress ended without ever getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Barbara Boxer introduced the bill on February 20, 1990, as the sole sponsor, with no cosponsors joining her.
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the same day it was introduced.
On April 26, 1990, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards and the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, which was the last action it ever received.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill expired when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who retaliate against employees who report federal law violations were better off, because they never faced the new liability, investigations, and damages the bill would have created. Whistleblowers were left with whatever protections existing law already provided.

for.name: Rep. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no colleague signed on as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; forwarded it to two subcommittees on April 26, 1990, and never reported it out or scheduled a vote.

against.name: Rep. Augustus Hawkins
against.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Presided over the committee that never held a hearing or markup on the bill and let it die in subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded and no opposition is documented in the record; the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so neither party ever took a position on it.

industries.note: The bill would have exposed companies working under federal contracts and programs to Labor Department investigations, reinstatement and back-pay orders, attorney's fees, and punitive damages when they punish employees who report waste, fraud, or safety dangers. Their interest in avoiding that liability ran directly against the workers' interest in being able to report violations safely.

industries.industry: State and local governments as employers
industries.note: By defining 'employee' to include state, county, and city workers, the bill would have let their employees file federal retaliation complaints, giving governments a stake in defeating it. Public employees who report abuse of authority in federally connected programs would have gained a remedy they often lacked.

industries.industry: Employers generally with any federal nexus
industries.note: Any employer whose conduct connects to a federal program, federal authority, or federal contract could face complaints based on a worker's reasonable belief of mismanagement or waste, even short of an actual violation. Compliant employers that simply follow the law would face little practical risk.
